Split Screen: Different Teams
She used to know every play Noor would make. Now she has to ask.
Two rival captains, three months after the breakup, one finals week. Iris knows everything about Noor except who she is now.

Iris Chen captains Nova. Noor Haddad captains Vanta. They dated for a year, broke up three months ago, and both made the Circuit Finals in Seattle. Iris still orders Noor's drink, still knows her tells, still thinks knowing someone means not having to ask. You decide whether Iris can relearn Noor from the current chapter, and whether they can each win their own night.
The adult league coordinator who runs finals week, books the green rooms, and has seen both captains' faces when the bracket dropped.
If nobody acts, Iris keeps loving an old version of Noor, and the real one stops answering.

I Didn't Read It
Take back the notebook, unread
Team hotel, 14th-floor hallway
Monday, 11:20 PM
The 14th floor, where both finalists are staying because the league has a sense of humor. Noor is waiting outside Iris's door with a spiral notebook.
That's my strat book. Nova's whole last season. It's been in her apartment since the day I left.
I hold it out. The cover is still bent where I stepped on it moving boxes.
I didn't read it.
You used to know all of it.
That's the problem.
My hand stops halfway. If I take it, that's the last thing of mine at her place.
What does Iris do?
Take it back. Say thank you.
I take it. I don't flip through it to check. That would be insulting to both of us.
Thank you. For not reading it. And for keeping it anyway.
I nod once and walk back to my room. I don't slam the door. I think she notices.
Iris took back her strat book without checking it and thanked Noor for keeping it unread.
Take it. Ask to talk after finals.
I'll take it. And after finals, when we're not opponents, can we talk about why we stopped talking?
After finals. Not before. I'm not doing this with a bracket over my head.
Deal. I'll put it on the calendar. In pen.
Iris took the notebook and asked to talk after finals; Noor agreed, but not before.
Don't take it. You're not ready.
Keep it. I'm not ready to have everything back yet.
It's your team's playbook, Iris. I can't hold that during finals.
I take it down to the league desk and have it sealed in an envelope with her name on it. I text her the photo. Nothing else.
Iris refused the notebook; Noor had it sealed at the league desk under Iris's name.
Last Season
Ask what Noor likes now
The players' lounge at the arena
Tuesday, 12:30 PM
Lunch in the players' lounge. One long counter, two teams pretending not to watch each other. Iris gets to the register first. She always does.
I order for both of us without thinking. Turkey club, no tomato. Iced vanilla latte, extra shot. It comes out of me like a reflex.
I swap the latte for a hibiscus soda, pay the difference, and say nothing.
You liked that.
Last season.
It's been three months.
Things can happen without you watching.
Three months. She has a new drink. What else is new? What else did I miss?
What does Iris do?
Ask what she drinks now. Then listen.
Okay. Hibiscus soda. Since when? Tell me like I'm new here.
I touch the logo on my hoodie. My support player brought a case to bootcamp in August. I hated it for a week. Then I didn't.
Scrims end at four. There's a stairwell by loading dock B nobody uses. If you want to ask me something real, ask me there.
Iris asked how Noor started drinking hibiscus soda and listened; Noor invited her to the loading-dock stairwell at four.
Stop ordering for her. Ask later, alone.
Sorry. Reflex. I'll stop. I want to ask about the soda, but not with both teams listening.
I look at her longer than I mean to. That's new too.
Then ask me at four. Stairwell by loading dock B. Nobody uses it. Come alone.
Iris apologized for ordering and asked to talk privately; Noor told her to come alone to the loading-dock stairwell at four.
Stop guessing. Go eat with your team.
Got it. I'll stop guessing. I'm going to go eat with my team before I guess anything else wrong.
I carry my tray to Nova's end of the counter. I don't look back. It takes real concentration.
Twenty minutes later I send one text: Stairwell by loading dock B. 4 PM. If you want to stop guessing, ask.
Iris walked back to her team rather than keep guessing; Noor texted her an invitation to the stairwell at four.
Try Asking
Admit that knowing her doesn't mean not having to ask
Stairwell by loading dock B
Tuesday, 4:05 PM
Concrete stairs, a humming exit sign, the muffled thud of a sound check through the wall. Noor is sitting on the fourth step with two sodas.
I sit two steps down. Not next to her. I'm learning.
When we were together, I treated you like you were on my team. Your schedule. Your food. Your nights. I just folded you in.
I thought knowing you meant not having to ask.
Try asking.
I hand her the second soda. It's hibiscus. It's a test, and we both know it.
One question. The right one. Not the one I already know the answer to.
What does Iris ask?
Ask what she wants now. Right now.
I open the soda. I drink it. It's awful. I keep drinking it.
What do you want? Not last year. This week.
To win Saturday without you in my head. And then dinner. Somewhere you've never been.
Iris asked what Noor wants this week; Noor said to win clean, then dinner somewhere new.
Suggest pros only until the final.
Can we be just captains until Saturday? I don't trust myself to learn you and play you in the same week.
That's the smartest thing you've said in a year.
I stand up and take my soda with me. At the door I stop. Sunday, then. Ask me again Sunday.
Iris asked to stay professional until the final; Noor agreed and told her to ask again on Sunday.
Insist she still likes the old drink.
Come on. You don't actually like this. You liked the vanilla thing for two years. People don't just change.
I take the soda back out of her hand, gently, and stand up.
I did. That's what I came here to tell you. I'll see you Saturday, Captain.
Iris insisted Noor hadn't really changed; Noor took the soda back and left, and they parted as opponents.
Two Reservations
Keep the celebrations separate; confirm tomorrow on its own
The league coordinator's desk, hotel lobby
Friday, 9:10 PM, the night before the final
The coordinator's clipboard has two after-party bookings for Saturday night. Nova: rooftop, 30 people. Vanta: a back room at a noodle bar, 12 people.
I booked the rooftop weeks ago. I put Noor on the list. Plus one: nobody. It seemed obvious. It was obvious, last season.
I assumed you would come.
My team has a night too.
I take the pen and cross her name off my list. It looks smaller than I expected, crossed out.
Tomorrow?
Tomorrow I choose the place.
Send me the address.
A new one. You haven't been there.
What does Iris do?
Confirm tomorrow. Let her pick everything.
Tomorrow. Your place, your time, your menu. I will not order for you. I might order for me, badly.
I almost smile. I write the time on the back of her hand with the coordinator's pen: 7:30. Address to follow.
Iris took Noor off her party list and confirmed a separate dinner the day after the final, Noor's choice.
Ask for a late coffee after both parties.
What about 1 AM? After both parties. Ten minutes, one coffee, then we go back to our people.
No. Tomorrow means tomorrow. Tonight means my team.
Okay. No is an answer. I'm practicing hearing it.
Iris asked for a 1 AM coffee after the parties; Noor said no, and Iris accepted it and kept the next-day dinner.
Ask for no texts until after the final.
Then here's my ask. No texts until the final's over. Not even good luck. I need my head clean too.
I touch the logo on my hoodie, then nod.
Fair. Radio silence. Your address comes after the last round, not before.
Iris asked for no contact until the final ended; Noor agreed and will send the dinner address after the last round.
Win Clean
Compete for real. No gifts, no borrowed reads
Circuit Finals main stage, Seattle
Saturday, 8:40 PM
Twelve thousand seats. Two glass booths. The handshake at center stage lasts exactly as long as a handshake should.
Win clean.
You too.
Game five. Last round. 12–12. Noor is Vanta's last player alive, holding a corner Iris could draw in her sleep.
Dex, Nova's entry, hisses on comms: “She always peeks left when she's last alive. You told us that. At her birthday.”
I did. I learned that tell in her kitchen, not in a scrim. And my hands still want to go easy on her.
What does Iris do?
Play your own read. Take the shot.
I ignore the left. I play what I see today: fresh footsteps, a new angle she's never used. I wait. She commits. I take it.
Nova wins, 13–12. At the handshake Noor's grip is firm and short.
That wasn't the old tell. Good. That was yours.
Iris won the final 13–12 on her own read, not Noor's old private tell; Noor acknowledged it at the handshake.
Hold the setup your team drilled.
No reads, no heroics. I hold the setup we drilled a hundred times. It's solid. It's also exactly what Noor expects.
Overtime. Vanta takes it, 15–13. Noor's booth erupts. At the handshake, Noor holds on one beat longer than the cameras need.
You played it straight. Thank you. I needed that one to be real.
Iris played Nova's drilled setup with no private reads; Vanta won in overtime, 15–13, and Noor thanked her for a real match.
Spend your timeout banning that tell.
Timeout. Listen to me. Nobody uses anything I know about her life. Not now, not ever. If you do, you're off my team.
The timeout costs Nova its rhythm. Vanta wins, 13–12. In the booth, Dex takes off his headset and apologizes first.
I saw the timeout from my booth. I don't know what she said. I can guess.
Iris burned a timeout to forbid her team using Noor's private tell; Nova lost the rhythm and Vanta won 13–12.
Tonight Belongs to My Team
Respect separate nights: one team's party, the other's quiet
Backstage hallway between the green rooms
Saturday, 11:05 PM
Two green rooms, one hallway. Whatever the scoreboard said, one door is shaking with music and the other is shut, lights low.
I step out into the hallway for air. Noor is at her own door, hand on the handle, not going in yet.
Dinner tomorrow?
Tomorrow. Tonight belongs to my team.
Okay. Text me the place.
I nod. I don't go in. For three seconds we're just two people in a hallway, and nobody is keeping score.
Every part of me wants to follow her through that door. That's exactly why I can't.
What does Iris do?
Go back to your team. All the way.
I go back into my room and I'm fully there: every hug, every bad speech, every replay. I don't check my phone once.
At 2:14 AM a text arrives: an address in a neighborhood Iris has never been to, and one word. Tomorrow.
Iris spent the night fully with her team; Noor texted a new address for tomorrow at 2:14 AM.
Ask for one minute. Then go.
One minute. Not about the game. Just: are you okay?
I'm okay. I'll be more okay in there. Go, Iris.
I go. At the end of the hallway I look back, and she's still at the door, watching me leave. Then she goes in.
Iris asked one minute to check on Noor, then left when asked; Noor watched her go before rejoining her team.
Say you need tonight too. Phone off.
Good. Because I need tonight too. I'm turning my phone off. Send the place, but I won't see it till noon.
Something in my shoulders lets go. She's not waiting on me. She has her own night.
Noon, then. It'll be there.
Iris claimed her own night and switched her phone off until noon; Noor was relieved and promised the address would be waiting.
A Place You've Never Been
Spend time off the stage without asking for her playbook
A Georgian restaurant in the Central District

How my day was. Not what my next play is.

Where does Iris take it?
Listen all night. Then ask for a second date.

Iris listened to Noor's day without interrupting and asked for a second date; Noor said yes.
Suggest being friends through the off-season.

Iris admitted she couldn't stop trying to manage Noor; they split the check and ended the private relationship kindly.
Different Teams
Choose a new rhythm: dating, rivals, or a pause
League media room, joint interview

You Haven't Been Here
Iris stopped ordering, stopped guessing, and started asking. Noor keeps choosing places Iris has never been, and Iris keeps showing up hungry and curious, on a different team.
You haven't been here. That's why.
Once in a While
They stayed rivals, and good ones. Between splits, when neither has a match, Iris asks, and sometimes Noor says yes.
Ask me again next time. I like hearing it.
Clean Play Only
Iris took Noor's team time one more time without asking, and Noor ended the personal side of it. They still meet on stage, still shake hands, and still play each other clean.
I'll see you at spring split. Win clean.
